sentences.text: For easy reference and understanding, the provisions of law involved in the present case have been broadly classified into two categories i.e Criminal Conspiracy and Cheating.
Let us discuss these categories one by one hereinafter.
CRIMINAL CONSPIRACY 8.
The criminal conspiracy is a punishable offence under Section 120 B IPC, which is defined under Section 120A IPC.

In case titled as Rajendra alias Rajesh alias Raju v. State of NCT of Delhi (2019)
10 SCC 623, the hon'ble Apex Court has observed that it is trite law that the existence of three elements must be shown--a criminal object, a plan or a scheme embodying means to accomplish that object, and an agreement or understanding between two or more people to cooperate for the accomplishment of such object's.
9.

Further in the case of Yogesh v. State of Maharashtra [(2008) 10 SCC 394], the honble Supreme Court of India in reference to criminal conspiracy has observed as follows:
"...25.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Thus, it is manifest that the meeting of minds of two or more persons for doing an illegal act or an act by illegal means is sine qua non of the criminal conspiracy but it may ABHISHEK KUMAR KUMAR 2023.12.18 17:23:21 State Vs. Pardeep Kumar etc. +0530 Page No.4 of 18 not be possible to prove the agreement between them by direct proof.
Nevertheless, existence of the conspiracy and its objective can be inferred from the surrounding circumstances and the conduct of the accused.
But the incriminating circumstances must form a chain of events from which a conclusion about the guilt of the accused could be drawn.

It is well settled that an offence of conspiracy is a substantive offence and renders the mere agreement to commit an offence punishable, even if an offence does not take place pursuant to the illegal agreement..."

10. To summarize, criminal conspiracy is an independent offence, which is punishable separately and can be proved either by way of direct proof or circumstantial evidence, only if essential ingredients as mentioned under Section 120A IPC are fulfilled.
CHEATING 11.
The offence pertaining to cheating is covered under Chapter 17 of the IPC under the heading 'of offences against property' and is covered from Section 415 to 420 IPC.
Section 420 i.e 'cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property' is an aggravated form of cheating, which provides for enhanced punishment.

12. In the offence of cheating, a person deceives another person fraudulently or dishonestly to deliver any property or consent to the retention of any property or intentionally induces another person to do or omit to do anything which he would not have done if he was not so deceived and State vs Pardeep Kumar Etc on 18 December, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/165312447/

In the case of Iridium India Tel oftenecom Ltd. v. Motorola Inc., (2011) 1 SCC 74, the Honble Supreme Court of India while refering to Section 415 IPC has observed as follows:
"...68.

sentences.text: A bare perusal of the aforesaid section would show that it can be conveniently divided into two parts.
The first part makes it necessary that the deception by the accused of the person deceived, must be fraudulent or dishonest.

Such deception must induce the person deceived to either: (a) deliver property to any person; or (b)
consent that any person shall retain any property.
The second part also requires that the accused must by deception intentionally induce the person deceived either to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit, if he was not so deceived.
Furthermore, such act or omission must cause or must be likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property.

Thus, it is evident that deception is a necessary ingredient for the offences of cheating under both parts of this section..."

sentences.text: Concerning the case against Rajender Kumar, the prosecution hinges on a conspiracy charge.

The pivotal question is whether the prosecution has proven that convict Pardeep Kumar and accused Rajender Kumar conspired to arrange the passport in question as well as accused Rajender Kumar facilitating Pardeep Kumar's journey after accepting Rs.5,00,000 on account of their alleged conspiracy.
22. The investigating officer's rationale for charging the accused with the conspiracy offense relies on three key factors.

Firstly, convict Pardeep Kumar identifying the accused Rajender Kumar as the agent; secondly, a hotel employee stating that accused Rajender booked a room in the name of Pardeep Kumar; and thirdly, a raid at Rajender Kumar's office, where photographs of the convict were discovered.
Let's analyze these facts that led to the alleged commission of the conspiracy offense and the involvement of accused Rajender Kumar.
The testimony of relevant witnesses and arguments pertaining to these points will be discussed afterwards.

23. The prosecution has examined two witnesses to establish fact of booking & payment at M/s.
Prince International hotel.
PW-3 Dollar Gulati testified that in 2006, he was the proprietor ABHISHEK KUMAR KUMAR
On 11.05.2006, Pardeep Kumar booked room no. 202, stayed with his wife, and checked out on 01.06.2006.
The IO seized attested photocopies of the entry register and bill (Ex.PW3/A) in Gulati's presence.
The original bill was exhibited as Ex.PW3/B (OSR), and the relevant entry from the register was exhibited as Ex.PW3/C (OSR).
However, Gulati's statement only confirmed Pardeep Kumar's stay at the hotel and did not implicate accused Rajender Kumar in any way regarding the hotel room booking in Pardeep Kumar's name.
24. Therefore, the testimony of PW-4 Gambhir Singh Chauhan becomes relevant as he was working in the hotel as a Manager in the year 2006.
The witness had given statement to the police officials which was exhibited as Ex.PW4/A during recording of his evidence.

Initially, the witness did not state the name of accused Rajender Kumar but upon putting leading questions to the witness with the permission of the Court, he stated that he might have told to the police officials that room no.202 in the hotel was booked and the payment was made by accused Rajender.
The witness was cross-examined at length by the counsel for the accused.
The witness admitted during the cross- examination that there was no name or signature of the accused Rajender Kumar in the Ex.PW3/B and Ex.PW3/C.
He also admitted the suggestion that there was no document which could confirm or show that the payment for the stay of the convict Pardeep Kumar was made by accused Rajender Kumar.

The witness could not identify the accused Rajender Kumar in the Court and stated that he may have seen the accused Rajender ABHISHEK KUMAR KUMAR Date:

Though he voluntarily stated that the payment was made by Rajender Kumar.

sentences.text: Upon careful scrutiny of PW-4's testimony, it is evident that it contains material inconsistencies.
The witness's account does not align with the documentary proof, which indicates that accused Rajender Kumar neither booked the hotel room nor made any payment on behalf of convict Pardeep Kumar.
Additionally, the witness's testimony lacks a categorical statement that accused Rajender Kumar was involved in the hotel booking; rather, it emphasizes the term 'may.'
The witness's inability to identify the accused in court, coupled with his statement only after leading questions were posed, raises doubts about the reliability of his testimony.
Consequently, the prosecution has failed to establish that accused Rajender Kumar played any role in the booking of the hotel room or its payment.
26. Now if we carefully scrutinize the testimony of PW-4, it will be found that the same suffers from material inconsistencies.

The testimony of the witness is not inconsonance with the documentary proof which states that the accused Rajender Kumar neither booked the hotel room nor made the payment on behalf of the convict Pardeep Kumar.
Further, the testimony of the witness does not categorically states that accused Rajender Kumar was involved in the booking of the hotel and emphasizes on the word 'may'.

Also, the witness could not identify the ABHISHEK KUMAR KUMAR Date:
2023.12.18 17:25:29 +0530 accused in the Court and had stated the name of the accused only after leading questions were put to him which makes his testimony doubtful and unreliable.
Therefore, the prosecution could not establish that accused Rajender Kumar had any role in the booking of the hotel room or its payment.

27. The counsel for the accused during the course of final arguments as well as in the cross-examination of the witnesses disputed the fact that the premises where the search was made,
did not belong to the accused and also the recovery of the photographs of the convict Pardeep Kumar, as alleged were not recovered from his possession.
He highlighted the contradictions amongst the prosecution witnesses with respect to the same.

In order to effectively address the arguments and contradictions raised by the counsel for the accused, reference to the testimonies of PW-6 ASI Rajender Kumar, PW-7 ASI Babu Ram and PW-11 Inspector Rajbir Singh is essential.
28. PW-6 ASI Rajender Kumar has deposed that on 05.06.2006, he was posted as Constable at PS Punjabi Bagh and was on picket duty at Club Road.
He along with SI Rajbir Singh and one Pardeep went to the H. NO.42, Second Floor, RWA Club Road, Punjabi Bagh for the search of office Mars Air Service Pvt. Ltd. at second floor.
After reaching there, SI Rajbir Singh gave his search to one independent witness namely Anil and he did not find anything from the possession of SI Rajbir Singh.

Thereafter, they took the search of the office and found one visiting card of Mars Air Service Pvt. Ltd and four passport size photographs of ABHISHEK KUMAR KUMAR 2023.12.18 17:25:41 +0530 Pardeep Kumar where accused Rajender Singh was also present.

sentences.text: After going through the testimony of above witnesses, some material contradictions have been found.
As per the version of the prosecution, PW-6 ASI Rajender Kumar and PW-7 ASI Babu Ram were the part of the raiding team.
However, the testimony of PW-6 points out that PW-7 ASI Babu Ram was not present there.
On the other hand, testimony of PW-7 reflects that PW-6 was not present at the time of search, raising serious doubt upon the version of the prosecution.

Further,
PW-6 stated that independent witness namely Anil was present at the time of the raid whereas PW-7 stated that no public person was there.

There is a material contradiction with respect to the fact that the IO had given his personal search before conducting the search in the premises at Punjabi Bagh as PW-6 states that IO gave the personal search but statement of PW-7 is contrary indicating no personal search was given by the IO.
PW-7 stated otherwise.

Also, the prosecution could not secure the attendance of the independent witness i.e. Anil during the prosecution evidence to prove the fact that IO has given his personal search to him as an independent witness.

Therefore, the testimony of witnesses have been found to be at variance with each other and the accused has ABHISHEK KUMAR KUMAR Date:
2023.12.18 17:26:10 +0530 been able to highlight the contradictions amongst these witnesses with respect to the raid at the Punjabi Bagh premises.

35. Even if, for the sake of argument, we overlook these contradictions, a crucial question arises i.e.
why did all members of the raiding party not undergo personal searches before entering the premises.
This raises concerns about the adherence to proper procedures, as solely relying on the personal search given by the IO does not validate the raid.
Prudence demands that each member of the raiding party should have undergone personal searches to eliminate suspicions, as asserted by the accused.
Importantly, no DD entry was produced to substantiate that the raid indeed took place at the Punjabi Bagh premises.
Moreover, there is no evidence to suggest that the premises belonged to accused Rajender Kumar, as no investigation in this regard was conducted by the IO.

Consequently, the prosecution falls short in proving that the raid was conducted at the Punjabi Bagh premises, that it belonged to the accused, or that the photographs and visiting card were genuinely recovered from the possession of accused Rajender Kumar, rather than being possibly planted on him.
36.

Since the basis on which the charge of conspiracy was alleged against accused Rajender Kumar remains unproved and the basis on which the investigation was conducted qua the accused Rajender Kumar was the disclosure statement of the convict Pardeep Kumar, the same cannot be read against the accused Rajender Kumar being inadmissible piece of evidence in ABHISHEK KUMAR KUMAR Date:
2023.12.18 17:26:20 +0530 the absence of corroboration from cogent/ material proof.
Also, there is no evidence to establish the fact that accused Rajender received an amount of Rs.5,00,000/- from the convict Pardeep Kumar except the inadmissible disclosure statement of the convict.

Moreover, the accused has succeeded to rebut the allegations levelled against him with respect to the conspiracy,
therefore, there is no requirement to delve into the aspects of his arrest etc. as the main allegations stands rebutted and the arrest of the accused was never disputed State vs Pardeep Kumar Etc on 18 December, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/165312447/
9 during the course of the trial except his involvement in facilitating the journey of the convict Pardeep Kumar or booking hotel room for him.

37. After examining the entire facts of the case in detail and concluding the facts which stands proved and disproved, let us now apply these facts to the provisions of law with which the accused has been charged and which shall be followed with the findings on the same hereinafter.
FINDING 38.
The main charge against the accused Rajender Kumar was the criminal conspiracy and upon the proof of the same, he could have been held liable for the substantive offence U/s.420 IPC.

As the charge of the conspiracy could not be established by the prosecution, therefore, the accused cannot be held liable in any manner whatsoever for the offence U/s.420 IPC.
39.

In view of the above discussion, I am of the firm opinion that the prosecution could not establish beyond reasonable doubt ABHISHEK KUMAR KUMAR 2023.12.18 17:26:35 +0530 that accused Rajender Kumar booked the hotel room for the convict Pardeep Kumar and made its payment.

Moreover, there is no proof that the premises bearing no.42, NWA, Club Road, Punjabi Bagh, Delhi belongs to the accused and the recovery of the photographs and the visiting card was effected from him.

To sum up, the prosecution could not establish the circumstances inferring the meeting of mind or agreement between the accused Rajender Kumar and the convict Pardeep Kumar to arrange the passport in question for the convict as well as facilitating his journey to Canada for a sum of Rs.5,00,000/-.

Accordingly, the accused stands acquitted for the offence under Section 120B and 420 r/w Section 120B IPC.
40.
Accused is directed to furnish bail bonds U/s.437A Cr.PC in the sum of Rs.10,000/-.
